pages.text: On Monday morning, the standpipe at Assin Nsuta JHS ran completely dry. Crossing the bridge earlier, Adwoa, Kwesi, and Musa had seen why: River Subin, once clear enough to show smooth pebbles on its bed, churned thick and yellowish-brown like cocoa drink. At assembly, the headteacher announced that illegal alluvial mining upstream had pushed the river’s turbidity so high that the district water treatment plant had shut its intake pumps to protect its machinery.

pages.alt: Three Ghanaian JHS students in yellow-and-brown uniforms stand safely on a concrete bridge looking down at a thick, yellowish-brown river.

pages.text: During Science, Mr Boateng placed a sealed jar of the muddy river water on the demonstration bench. Wearing gloves, Adwoa observed how fine clay and silt hung in the water. “Because insoluble solid particles are dispersed throughout the liquid without dissolving, this heterogeneous mixture is a suspension,” Mr Boateng explained. After letting the heaviest grit settle by sedimentation, Kwesi carefully decanted the cloudy top layer through a folded filter paper into a conical flask. Brown residue stayed on the paper, while clear liquid, the filtrate, dripped steadily below.

pages.alt: In a Ghanaian JHS science lab, Mr Boateng watches gloved Adwoa and Kwesi pour cloudy water through filter paper in a funnel into a conical flask.

pages.text: Kwesi held the flask up to the window. “Sir, the filtrate looks crystal clear! If we boil it to kill germs, is it safe to drink?” Mr Boateng shook his head firmly. “Never assume clear water is pure water, Kwesi. Filtration only traps insoluble suspended solids. Boiling destroys living pathogens such as cholera and typhoid bacteria, but it cannot destroy dissolved chemical pollutants or toxic heavy metals like mercury and lead used in illegal mining. Worse still, boiling evaporates pure water as steam and leaves dissolved heavy metals even more concentrated in the pot.”

pages.alt: Mr Boateng in a white lab coat holds up a warning finger beside a flask of clear filtrate and a wordless chalkboard icon diagram of droplets.

pages.text: In Social Studies that afternoon, the class traced the wider cost of river degradation across Ghana. When excavators strip away riverbanks and wash soil directly into streams, farmers downstream lose fertile cocoa and vegetable floodplains, fish habitats collapse, and towns spend far more public money on coagulants like alum to treat domestic water. Musa pointed to the district map: “Destroying a river for quick gold transfers massive health and economic costs onto innocent communities downstream.”

pages.text: On Wednesday, the school’s Environmental Club invited Nana Ofori to an RME forum on caring for creation. “Every moral tradition in Ghana teaches accountability for the Earth,” Musa noted. “Christianity teaches stewardship, that God entrusted creation to humans to tend and protect, and Islam teaches that we are Khalifah, trustees of Allah’s Earth who must never corrupt clean water.” Nana Ofori nodded warmly. “And our ancestors forbade farming or digging along riverbanks and set sacred rest days for rivers. Those taboos were not empty superstition; they preserved vegetated buffer zones that held the soil in place and filtered rainwater naturally.”

pages.text: Understanding the science, civic impact, and moral duty changed how the students acted. Working safely on dry school land with the Forestry Commission officer and local elders, never confronting illegal miners themselves, the club planted native trees and clumping bamboo fifty metres back from the town’s tributary stream to restore its protective buffer zone. At their Friday science exhibition, Adwoa shared a message the whole school remembered: “Filtration clears mud, and boiling kills germs, but only responsible stewardship keeps poison out of our water.”

activities.question: Why is muddy river water classified as a suspension rather than a solution?
options: Insoluble solid particles hang in the water and can settle or be filtered
All the soil has chemically bonded with water to form a new compound
It contains only pure distilled water and dissolved oxygen gas

activities.question: Why does boiling clear, filtered river water NOT make it safe if illegal mining chemicals are present?
options: Boiling kills germs, but dissolved heavy metals like mercury stay behind
Boiling turns insoluble sand particles back into thick brown mud
Filter paper adds toxic mercury to the water before it boils

activities.question: What ecological purpose did traditional riverbank taboos share with modern environmental laws?
options: Both protect vegetated buffer zones that stop riverbank erosion and mud
Both encourage digging closer to the riverbed during the dry season
Both allow waste disposal in streams on sacred rest days

activities.prompt: Put the scientific investigation and community action steps in chronological order.
items: High river turbidity forces the district water plant to shut its pumps.
Students separate silt by sedimentation, decantation, and filtration.
Mr Boateng explains why filtration and boiling leave heavy metals behind.
Students work with elders and forestry officers to replant a buffer zone.

activities.definition: The clear liquid that passes through a filter after solid residue is trapped.
distractors: The solid brown mud left behind on top of the filter paper
A chemical coagulant added to settle fine clay particles

glossary.definition: The cloudiness of water caused by large numbers of suspended particles such as silt and clay.
A heterogeneous mixture in which insoluble solid particles hang in a liquid and settle on standing.
The clear liquid collected after a mixture passes through a filter, which may still hold dissolved substances.
Disease-causing microorganisms, such as certain bacteria and viruses, destroyed by boiling or chlorination.
The moral duty to care for and protect God’s creation and natural resources for future generations.
